newsitem.title: UK: British opposition calls for tougher sleaze probe.
newsitem.headline: British opposition calls for tougher sleaze probe.

text.p: Britain's main opposition parties pressed the government on Monday to step up inquiries into allegations of parliamentary sleaze involving a former minister.

Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats said they were afraid a parliamentary watchdog set up after a wave of sleaze scandals did not have sufficient powers for an in-depth inquiry into the allegations about former trade minister Neil Hamilton.

The parties' chief whips, their parliamentary managers, told a news conference they were also worried about allegations ruling Conservative party managers sought to influence a key committee which governs the conduct of members of parliament.
"It is important that the scope of the enquiry should be comprehensive," said Labour chief whip Donald Dewar.

Dewar and the Liberal Democrat whip, Archie Kirkwood, said Sir Gordon Downey, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards -- a post set up after a sleaze inquiry last year sparked by the case -- should have more resources and more powers if needed.

They also said MPs would be requesting an investigation by the House of Commons speaker into whether David Willetts, then a government whip but now a treasury minister, broke parliamentary rules by suggesting a key committee should clear Hamilton.
"The allegations and complaints on both matters must be thoroughly and rigorously investigated...Public opinion demands it and the reputation of our democratic system deserves it," Dewar said.
The move, which comes the day parliament resumes after the summer break, was designed to keep up pressure on the government in the run-up to an election now no more than seven months away.
It was given added weight by the weekend decision of rebel Conservative MP Peter Thurnham to join the Liberal Democrats in protest at Prime Minister John Major's handling of sleaze.

Aides to Major said an earlier request from Labour and the Liberal Democrats for a totally independent judicial inquiry had beenn rejected on legal grounds as it would require a change in the law, a decision Kirkwood described as regrettable.
But the aide said: "The prime minister is extremely keen that these matters should be addressed as quickly as possible."
Senior Conservative MPs have been outraged by the move, which they said was motivated by a desire to score political points off the government and not a concern for ethics.
Conservative MP Paul Marland told the BBC: "I'm astonished that the Labour party and the Liberals are actually taking this issue up again...It doesn't do parliament any good.
The new outbreak of conflict follows successful annual party conferences for both Labour and the Conservatives.

Major pulled his party together and gave an image of unity at his conference last week, portraying himself as an honest, down-to-earth leader. He also bitterly attacked the opposition for their campaign to portray his government as sleazy.
But Labour, whose disciplined party conference boosted their already huge opinion poll lead, believes the ruling party is very vulnerable to charges of sleaze after 17 years in office.
Major has a parliamentary majority of just two. Although it is unlikely Major could be brought down over the current argument, a call for a vote of no confidence could be damaging.
Labour leader Tony Blair, on a tour of South Africa, on Sunday left the option open. "We will have to wait and see how the debate progresses. I don't rule anything out," he said.
The latest case involves allegations that former trade minister Neil Hamilton accepted cash in return for asking parliamentary questions in breach of House of Commons rules.

Hamilton has denied the charges. But two weeks ago he dropped a libel action against the Guardian newspaper which broke the story. Hamilton said he could not afford the legal fees, but the Guardian responded by printing fresh allegations.
